Module 15
Fauvism: Bold Color and Raised Texture
Lesson
📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
What happens when an artist stops using "real" colors on purpose?
A little over a hundred years ago, a group of painters in France shocked everyone by using wild, unrealistic color. A face could be green. The sea could be pink. Critics were so surprised they called the painters fauves, the French word for wild beasts, and the name stuck. Today you meet their leader, Henri Matisse, and then you will plan a project that adds a second kind of boldness: raised texture you can feel with your fingers.
✅ BY THE END OF THIS MODULE, YOU WILL BE ABLE TO
☐ Explain what Fauvism is and describe how its painters used bold, non-realistic color on purpose.
☐ Connect Henri Matisse's work to the time and place it came from, France, in the early 1900s A.D.
☐ Plan and build a foil embossing that combines raised texture with bold, non-realistic color.
⚡ QUICK CHECK-IN
Before you read on: if you painted a picture of yourself using colors that did NOT match real life, which color would you reach for first? (No wrong answer. Just check in with yourself.)
📚 PART 1 · MEET THE WILD BEASTS

Henri Matisse and Fauvism

Henri Matisse (1869 to 1954 A.D.) was a French artist known for bright color, simple shapes, and a creative, free style. He became the leader of Fauvism, an art movement that came after Post-Impressionism in the early 1900s A.D.

Fauvist painters were not trying to make art look real. They used bright, unrealistic colors, simple shapes, and strong, visible brushstrokes to show feeling and energy. Matisse asked a daring question: what if color does not have to match real life?

💡 KEY IDEA
Fauvism = bold, non-realistic color used on purpose. The color is chosen for feeling, not for accuracy.
👁 PART 2 · LOOK CLOSELY

Henri Matisse, Woman with a Hat

In this 1905 A.D. portrait, a woman sits turned slightly to one side wearing a large, heavy hat. Look closely. Her face is not painted in skin tones. Streaks of green, yellow, and pink run across it. The hat piles up in purple, blue, teal, and orange. Even the background is split into patches of green, pink, and orange. None of the color is realistic, and that is the point.

Henri Matisse, Woman with a Hat, 1905. Public domain (published before 1930).
🔍 WHAT TO NOTICE
Bold, non-realistic color on the face and hat. Loose, visible brushstrokes you can almost feel. Simple, flat shapes instead of careful detail. When it was first shown, many viewers were upset and thought it looked unfinished and strange.
📚 PART 3 · COLOR ACROSS HIS WORK

A landscape: The Sea Seen at Collioure

In this 1906 A.D. seaside view, a dark tree branch arches across the top and a trunk rises at the right. The sea is a band of teal and blue, and the ground in front is loose patches of pink, green, and orange sitting side by side. The land is painted bright pink rather than brown, another Fauvist color choice.

Henri Matisse, The Sea Seen at Collioure, 1906. Public domain (published before 1930).

An early work: Still Life with Compote

From 1899 A.D., before full Fauvism, this tabletop shows a footed bowl (a compote) of fruit, a dark green bottle, and a pink-and-white cup on a yellow-streaked table, all against a dappled pink wall. The color is already warm and lively, hinting at where his bolder choices would go.

Henri Matisse, Still Life with Compote, 1899. Public domain (published before 1930).
⚡ TAP TO REVEAL
Where does the word Fauvism come from? (Tap to find out.)
From the French word fauves, meaning wild beasts. Critics used it to mock the wild, unrealistic color, but the artists kept the name.
📚 PART 4 · ADD A SECOND KIND OF BOLD

Texture and relief

Texture is one of the seven Elements of Art. It is how a surface feels, or looks like it would feel. A relief is artwork with raised parts that stand up off a flat surface, so the texture is real, not just a drawn illusion.

Your Studio Project is a foil embossing. You will glue raised lines onto a flat board, press shiny foil over them so the lines rise up as real bumps, and then color the foil with bold, Fauvist color. Two bold ideas in one piece: raised texture you can feel and non-realistic color you can see.

🟫 HOW EMBOSSING MAKES TEXTURE
Anything raised under the foil, like a line of yarn, pushes the foil up. Run your finger over the finished piece and you feel every raised line. That is relief: texture you can touch.
